message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of tasks:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from operating system tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel processing – originally built to render graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each highly optimized for complex control flow, low latency, and large caches. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores, optimized for throughput and data‑parallel workloads. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set architecture (CISC) like x86 or ARM; supports branching, recursion, and varied memory access patterns. | SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) style; many cores execute the same operation on different data simultaneously. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution. | Smaller per‑core cache, relies on massive bandwidth from shared memory; less emphasis on latency. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Single‑threaded or lightly threaded tasks, I/O bound operations, OS kernel work, database queries. | Highly parallel tasks: rendering pixels/vertices, matrix multiplications, convolutional neural networks, simulations. |
| **Performance Metrics** | Clock speed (GHz), instructions per cycle (IPC), single‑thread performance. | FLOPS (floating‑point ops per second), memory bandwidth, throughput. |
| **Energy Efficiency** | Optimized for low power per core when idle, high power when busy. | High raw throughput but often higher power draw; modern GPUs have power‑management features. |

In short, CPUs excel at handling diverse, sequential tasks quickly, while GPUs shine at performing the same operation on many pieces of data at once—making them ideal for graphics, deep learning, and other massively parallel computations.
